Eliphal
EL-i-fal
n. (proper name; son of Ur, among David's mighty men)
Hebrew 'Eliphal, commonly read God hath judged or whom God judges, from 'el (God) with a root for judging or pleading a cause. The margin of 1 Chronicles 11:35 offers the variant Eliphelet.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · In the Text · Related

Biblical Definition

Eliphal is named once: “Ahiam the son of Sacar the Hararite, Eliphal the son of Ur” (1 Chronicles 11:35). The parallel roll in 2 Samuel 23:34 gives the corresponding place in the list to “Eliphelet the son of Ahasbai, the son of the Maachathite,” and the margin of the Chronicles verse notes both variants. The dictionary records the difference without alarm. Two rolls of the same company, compiled at different times and perhaps from different musters, will differ in some names and patronymics; the Masoretic text preserves what it received, and nothing doctrinal depends on which form stood in the original register. What the name says is worth more than the spelling: God hath judged. In David's mouth that was the whole ground of his cause. He would not stretch out his hand against Saul and said so in the words of a man content to be judged rather than to judge: “The LORD judge between me and thee, and the LORD avenge me of thee: but mine hand shall not be upon thee” (1 Samuel 24:12). A man of that company named God hath judged carried his captain's doctrine in his name.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): Eliphal is a Hebrew proper name and has no entry in Webster's dictionary of the English language.

expand to see more

Eliphal is a Hebrew proper name; Webster's 1828 dictionary treats common English words and does not define it.

The name appears once, in 1 Chronicles 11:35.

He is named as the son of Ur, among David's mighty men.

The margin of the verse offers the variants Eliphelet and Ahasbai.

The name is commonly read God hath judged.

Key Scripture

1Ch 11:35 — "Ahiam the son of Sacar the Hararite, Eliphal the son of Ur,"

2Sa 23:34 — "Eliphelet the son of Ahasbai, the son of the Maachathite, Eliam the son of Ahithophel the Gilonite,"

1Sa 24:12 — "The LORD judge between me and thee, and the LORD avenge me of thee: but mine hand shall not be upon thee."

Psa 7:8 — "The LORD shall judge the people: judge me, O LORD, according to my righteousness, and according to mine integrity that is in me."

Modern Corruption

Variant names in parallel musters are urged as proof the text is unreliable; the variation touches no doctrine at all.

expand to see more

Where 2 Samuel 23 and 1 Chronicles 11 differ in a name or a father's name, the difference is regularly presented as evidence that the records are untrustworthy. The dictionary holds providential preservation and reads the difference as what it is. Two musters of one company, taken at different dates, will not match name for name, and the Masoretic tradition hands down both with the margins noting the alternatives.

The principle to recover is a doctrine of Scripture strong enough to be honest. The Bible's authority does not rest on the claim that no name was ever written two ways; it rests on God's preservation of His word, which the marginal apparatus serves rather than threatens. A reader who demands a text with no variants will end by distrusting the text he has.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew 'Eliphal, God hath judged; son of Ur in the roll of David's mighty men, with the variant Eliphelet.

expand to see more

Hebrew 'Eliphal, from 'el (God) with a root for judging.

The sense is God hath judged, or whom God judges.

He is named the son of Ur, 1 Chronicles 11:35.

The margin offers Eliphelet for the name and Ahasbai for the father.

2 Samuel 23:34 gives Eliphelet the son of Ahasbai in the parallel place.
